criterion_notes.c1: Examines household sanitation service access in India, including types of toilet facilities used by households and open defecation prevalence.
criterion_notes.c2: Fails both the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading and the plain wording of Criterion 2 as an empirical exposure. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 reading, the empirical analysis (NFHS-4 tabulations and binary logistic regression) examines only household wealth index and urban/rural locality rather than any rule-type mechanism governing service access (such as eligibility screening, administrative burden, tenure/documentation rules, tariffs, discretion, enforcement, or regulatory structure). Although the narrative sections on product and process innovation briefly mention anecdotal examples (government manual specifications for subsidy verification, a proposed 2019 parliamentary bill prohibiting open defecation, and a Gram Panchayat rule denying haircuts and tea), these are unanalysed illustrative remarks within a broad social-innovation essay focused on toilet technology, behaviour-change communication, stakeholder collaboration, and R&D output. Under the plain wording of Criterion 2, while the narrative text touches broadly on institutional constraints and public sanitation programmes, no legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory, or governance factor is empirically examined or linked to sanitation access outcomes, so the paper is excluded under the plain reading as well.
criterion_notes.c3: Contains secondary quantitative empirical evidence in the form of NFHS-4 (2014-15) household sanitation tabulations and a binary logistic regression of improved toilet use on wealth categories and urban residence (plus Scopus bibliometric publication counts from 1969-2020), whereas the discussion of social innovation, institutions, and policy is purely narrative commentary with no primary data or empirical evaluation.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports household access to improved sanitation facilities (by toilet technology) and open defecation rates from NFHS-4 (2014-15).
criterion_notes.c5: While the NFHS-4 secondary analysis identifies households in India (without reporting sample size or methods details), socioeconomic/locality predictors, and improved toilet access, the paper provides no identifiable empirical study design, sample, exposure measurement, or outcome evaluation for any legal, governance, or innovation factor.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is written in English (with an additional Polish abstract/title translation).

raw_response.exposure: Household wealth index (poorest, poorer, middle, richer, richest) and household locality (urban vs. rural) in the empirical NFHS-4 analysis; conceptual narrative discussion of product and process social innovations
raw_response.outcome: Household access to improved toilet facilities (flush to piped sewer, septic tank, VIP latrine, pit latrine with slab, etc.) and open defecation prevalence
raw_response.population_and_sample: Households in India in the National Family Health Survey (NFHS-4, 2014-15; exact sample size not reported); also Scopus-indexed Indian sanitation publications (1969-2020, n = 1,628)
raw_response.rationale: Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure). The paper's empirical sanitation-access component (secondary NFHS-4 descriptive tabulations and binary logistic regression in Figure 1 and Tables 1-2) examines only household wealth index and urban/rural residence as predictors of improved toilet access and open defecation, rather than any legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory, or governance factor. Its main discussion of 'social innovation' (eco-toilets, product design, behaviour-change communication, R&D bibliometrics, and passing anecdotal mentions of subsidy manuals, a 2019 parliamentary bill, and a village panchayat rule) is a non-empirical narrative overview with no empirical method or data testing any rule-type mechanism governing service access.
raw_response.study_design: Cross-sectional secondary survey data analysis (NFHS-4 descriptive statistics and binary logistic regression) combined with narrative policy/innovation overview and Scopus bibliometric counts
